Reference

Vocabulary bank

Collocations, phrasal verbs, discourse markers and idioms from the lessons: what they mean and how they sound on screen.

Intensifying collocations

From Lesson 3.

ItemMeaningOn screen example
bitterly disappointedvery disappointed, with a sense of hurt"I was bitterly disappointed when they cancelled it."
highly unlikelyalmost certainly won't happen"Him, apologising? That's highly unlikely."
utterly ridiculouscompletely absurd (utterly mostly with negative words)"The whole thing was utterly ridiculous."
deeply regretsincerely regret (formal or serious apology)"I deeply regret what I said."
fully awarecompletely aware (often defensive)"Yes, I'm fully aware it's my fault."
strongly suspectbe fairly sure, without proof"I strongly suspect he's been reading my messages."
painfully obviousso clear it's awkward or embarrassing"It was painfully obvious he fancied her."
perfectly normalnot strange at all (reassuring)"It's perfectly normal to feel nervous."
very + gradable adjectiveordinary adjectives with degrees: very tired / angry / good"I'm very tired, let's go home."
absolutely + extreme adjectivenot very: absolutely exhausted / furious / brilliant; really works with both"She wasn't angry. She was absolutely furious."

Phrasal verbs in dialogue

From Lesson 5.

ItemMeaningOn screen example
fall out (with sb)argue and stop being friends · never split"He fell out with his dad years ago."
make up (UK also make it up)forgive each other after an argument · no object"They always kiss and make up."
let sb downdisappoint sb by not doing what you promised · separable"You promised. Don't let me down."
put up withaccept something or someone unpleasant · never split"I don't know why she puts up with him."
wind sb up (UK informal)1 annoy sb · 2 tell sb something untrue as a joke · separable"Are you winding me up?"
get away withavoid punishment for something wrong · never split"How does he get away with it?"
come up withthink of an idea or plan · never split"Has anyone come up with anything?"
bring sth upstart talking about a subject · separable"Whatever you do, don't bring it up."
pick up onnotice something others missed or that wasn't said directly"Did anyone else pick up on that?"
come across asgive the impression of being"She comes across as a bit cold."
Word orderpronoun goes in the middle of separable verbs; verbs ending in a preposition keep the object after it"bring it up" · "put up with it"

Discourse markers

From Lesson 6.

ItemWhat the speaker is doingOn screen example
mind you (mainly UK)contrasting: making what they just said less strong"He's untidy. Mind you, I'm not much better."
having said thatcontrasting: despite what I've just said"I hate musicals. Having said that, I loved Hamilton."
then again / there againcontrasting: a new, opposite thought"I'd love a dog. Then again, who'd walk it?"
Still, (front position)contrasting: nevertheless"It rained all week. Still, we had a laugh."
to be fairconceding: admitting a point on the other side"To be fair, they were short-staffed."
fair enough (UK informal)conceding: I understand your reason"It's Mum's birthday." "Oh, fair enough."
actuallycorrecting politely, or giving a surprising fact · not "currently""Kraków, actually."
I meancorrecting yourself or adding detail; also a filler"It's Friday. I mean Saturday."
as it happensrevealing a fact that is relevant by chance"As it happens, my brother's a plumber."
anywaychanging topic, returning to the main topic, or wrapping up"Anyway, enough about me. How's the job?"

Idioms in conversation

From Lesson 10.

ItemMeaningOn screen example
the last straw (also the final straw)the latest problem that makes a situation impossible to accept"He didn't even call. That's the last straw."
be (skating) on thin icebe in a risky position, close to trouble"One more complaint and you're out. You're on thin ice."
take the mickey / mick (out of sb)UK, informal: tease or make fun of someone"Are you taking the mickey?"
the elephant in the rooman obvious problem nobody wants to discuss"Are we going to talk about the elephant in the room?"
beat around the bush (UK also beat about the bush)avoid talking about what is important"Stop beating about the bush. Am I fired?"
jump the gundo something too soon, without thinking"Three weeks and he's looking at rings? He's jumping the gun."
call it a dayinformal: stop what you're doing (for now); also retire"We're all knackered. Let's call it a day."
cut sb some slackinformal: judge someone less harshly"Cut him some slack, he's only been here a week."
not be sb's cup of teanot the kind of thing someone likes"Horror films aren't really my cup of tea."
a blessing in disguisesomething that seems bad at first but has a good result"Losing that job was a blessing in disguise."

Updated as lessons add new vocabulary. Check meanings and levels in the Cambridge Dictionary and the English Vocabulary Profile.
